newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai market seen going down in week ahead.
newsitem.headline: Thai market seen going down in week ahead.

text.p: The Thai market is seen edging down next week as poor macroeconomic figures and doubts surrounding the viability of a property support scheme continue to dampen sentiment, analysts said on Friday.
The SET Index closed on Friday at 709.09, up 6.99 points or 1.00 percent, from the previous Friday's close.
The market's potential downside is limited but there is little positive news waiting to signal a rebound.

"I still think the market will move just like this (past) week, I think it will go down or at best move sideways because we are not looking forward to any positive news next week," said Tom Paiboon, head of research at TISCO.
The Easter holiday on Monday and the Thai New Year holiday next weekend are likely to keep trade quiet.
A feeling the worst is over has inspired some major brokers like WI Carr, Merill Lynch and SBC Warburg to upgrade their recommendations on the Thai market.
But most investors are waiting for more concrete evidence of a turnaround before committing to the market, analysts said.

"These calls seem a little premature. We think interest rate pressure will continue to build up and there are still concerns about asset quality," said James Marshall, head of research at Capital Nomura Securities.
Among concerns likely to limit market gains were central bank figures released on Thursday showing January's current account deficit and trade deficit had widened month on month.
High lending rates, which at over 13 percent are among the highest in Asia, are also likely to remain high, analysts said.
Those rates are required to attract foreign capital to finance the current account deficit and defend the baht, but are stifling the economy.
A number of firms have revised economic growth projections down over the last two weeks to around five percent from near seven percent.

Some downside factors like a possible Moody's downgrade of the country's long term A2 sovereign rating, and poor first quarter earnings have been discounted by the market. But asset quality fears and questions over the viability of a 100 billion baht bond funded government property bailout means the upside is limited, brokers said.
"The bottom of the market is probably not too far away, but it's a question of when the upside potential is going to be realised," said Jim Landi, head of research at Vickers Ballas.
